title: What If Your Children Reject God?
paragraphs: What If Your Children Reject God?

You taught them to pray. You brought them to church. You whispered the name of Jesus over their crib. But what happens when the child you raised to know God looks you in the eyes and says, “I don’t believe anymore”?
There is a sentence some Christian parents are terrified they will hear.
Maybe you have already heard it.
“I don’t believe in God anymore.”
Sometimes it comes dramatically. Sometimes it arrives quietly.
A Bible left unopened.
Church attendance becomes an argument.
Prayer becomes awkward.
Questions become skepticism.
The worship songs they once sang disappear from their playlist. The child who once folded tiny hands beside the bed now rolls their eyes when you mention Jesus.
And perhaps the hardest part is that you remember.
You remember teaching them, “Jesus loves me.”
You remember their first children’s Bible.
You remember hearing their little voice pray.
You remember the Sunday-school crafts stuck to the refrigerator.
You remember the day they asked whether Jesus could really hear them.
You said yes.
You believed they believed you.
And now you lie awake wondering...
What happened?
Then comes the question beneath the question.
Was it me?
Maybe I failed.
Maybe I was too strict.
Maybe I wasn’t strict enough.
Maybe they saw too much hypocrisy in me.
Maybe I should have prayed more.
Maybe I should have explained Scripture better.
Maybe I worked too much.
Maybe I pushed church too hard.
Maybe I didn't push hard enough.
Maybe...
Maybe...
Maybe...
And before long, you are no longer simply grieving for your child.
You are prosecuting yourself.
But if your son or daughter is wandering from God, there are truths you desperately need to understand before guilt turns your prayer life into a courtroom.

Scripture commands parents to teach their children faithfully. Deuteronomy 6 says God's words are first to be upon the parent's own heart and then taught diligently to the children—in ordinary life, sitting at home, walking along the way, lying down, and rising.
The Hebrew wording is beautiful.
וְשִׁנַּנְתָּם לְבָנֶיךָ
Veshinnantam levaneikha.
“And you shall teach them diligently to your children.”

The picture is not merely of mentioning God occasionally. The command carries the force of impressing His words deeply—sharpening them, repeating them, bringing God's truth into the rhythm of ordinary life.
Christian parenting was never supposed to mean outsourcing discipleship to a church building for ninety minutes every Sunday.
It means Jesus at the dinner table.
Jesus in disappointment.
Jesus after failure.
Jesus when prayers appear unanswered.
Jesus when Dad has to apologize.
Jesus when Mom is exhausted.
Jesus when somebody sins.
Jesus when somebody forgives.
Jesus when the family has money.
Jesus when the family doesn't.
Jesus when life makes sense.
And Jesus when life hurts so badly that nobody knows what to say.
But here is where some devastated parents have unintentionally wounded themselves with another verse.
“Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it.” — Proverbs 22:6, KJV.
They read that proverb as though God signed an unconditional contract:
If I parent correctly, my child can never reject Christ.
Then their child wanders.
And the conclusion becomes unbearable.
Therefore, I must have failed.

But Proverbs are wisdom sayings describing the normal patterns and consequences of wise living; they should not automatically be treated as unconditional promises eliminating human responsibility or every possible exception. The Hebrew verb חָנַךְ (ḥānak) in Proverbs 22:6 carries the sense of training or dedicating. The NET Bible's notes likewise caution against treating the proverb as though exceptions cannot occur.
That matters enormously.
Because parents have responsibility.
But parents do not possess sovereignty over another human heart.
You can teach truth.
You cannot manufacture regeneration.
You can bring your child to church.
You cannot bring the Holy Spirit into their heart by force.
You can explain the Gospel.
You cannot repent on their behalf.
You can put Scripture before their eyes.
You cannot make them love what they read.
You can model Christ imperfectly but sincerely.
You cannot believe for them.
Christian parents are called to faithful discipleship, not divine control.
Only God is God.
And strangely, admitting that may be one of the most freeing and terrifying moments of parenthood.
Because eventually the little hand you once held must make real decisions.
Your child is not your spiritual trophy.
Your child's salvation is not evidence that you were a perfect parent, and your child's wandering does not automatically prove that you were a terrible one.
That does not mean parents should refuse honest self-examination.
Quite the opposite.
Maybe there are things you need to repent of.
Maybe your children heard you preach grace but experienced anger.
Maybe they saw Christianity used more often as a weapon than as good news.
Maybe the house had Bible verses hanging on the walls while bitterness lived at the dinner table.
Maybe “because the Bible says so” became a substitute for listening to painful questions.
Maybe maintaining the appearance of a Christian family became more important than cultivating a home where confession was safe.
If so...
don't defend it.
Repent.
One of the most powerful testimonies a parent can give a doubting child may not be another sermon.
It may be:
“I was wrong.”
“I hurt you.”
“I represented Christ poorly there.”
“Please forgive me.”
“I cannot undo what I did, but I want Jesus to change me.”
That is not weakness.
That is Christianity.
Because the Gospel was never about pretending Christians don't sin.
The Gospel announces what God has done about sinners.
Paul describes believers as people reconciled to God through Christ and entrusted with the message of reconciliation.
That means your home does not need a flawless Christian performance.
It needs the aroma of repentance.
Your children should see what happens when Christians fail.
We confess.
We repent.
We seek forgiveness.
We make restitution where possible.
We get back up.
We run to Christ.
And perhaps your child needs to discover that the Jesus they rejected is not necessarily the Jesus who actually exists.
Sometimes people reject a caricature.
A political mascot.
A religious culture.
A hypocritical church experience.
A harsh father projected onto God.
A prosperity formula that failed them.
A shallow Christianity unable to survive suffering.
A version of faith that treated questions as rebellion.
Don't panic at every question.
Listen.
Ask what they mean.
“What happened?”
“What made believing difficult?”
“Did someone hurt you?”
“What do you think Christianity claims?”
“What do you think about Jesus Himself?”
Then listen long enough to hear the answer you were afraid to hear.
You are not betraying truth by listening.
Truth does not become fragile because someone questions it.
And while you listen, remember something astonishing about Jesus.
He already knows.
He knows the argument your child has not told you about.
He knows the wound behind the sarcasm.
He knows what happened at college.
He knows what happened online.
He knows the disappointment.
He knows the temptation.
He knows the secret.
He knows whether intellectual objections are genuine, whether moral resistance is involved, whether church wounds are bleeding underneath the anger—or whether several things are tangled together.
You see a closed bedroom door.
Christ sees the heart behind it.
So pray.
Not the manipulative prayer of panic.
Not, “God, make my child behave so I won't be embarrassed.”
Pray for resurrection.
Pray for conviction.
Pray for mercy.
Pray that false ideas collapse.
Pray that hidden wounds come into the light.
Pray that Christians with genuine humility cross their path.
Pray that the emptiness of idols becomes obvious.
Pray that they encounter Scripture when they least expect it.
Pray that memories of truth return at strange hours of the night.
Pray that the Holy Spirit does what arguments alone never could.
And while you pray...
keep loving them.
This does not mean approving everything.
Love and agreement are not synonyms.
Jesus never required moral confusion in order to demonstrate compassion.
You can say, “I believe this is wrong,” without saying, “You are no longer welcome at my table.”
You can hold conviction without cruelty.
You can refuse to compromise Scripture without turning every family gathering into an interrogation.
You can stop trying to win every argument so that you do not lose every conversation.
Remember the story Jesus told about a father and a wandering son.
The younger son walked away.
The father did not pretend the rebellion was righteousness.
But neither did he extinguish his love.
And then comes one of the most emotionally devastating scenes in Scripture.
Luke tells us that while the son was still far away, his father saw him, felt compassion, ran to him, embraced him, and kissed him.
The father's running did not make the rebellion good.
It revealed that mercy was waiting when repentance brought the wanderer home.
That is the Gospel-shaped tension.
Truth does not disappear.
Sin does not become harmless.
Repentance still matters.
But grace stands at the road watching.
Perhaps tonight you are standing at that road.
Your child still has not come home spiritually.
And this is where I refuse to sell you a sentimental ending Scripture does not promise me I can guarantee.
I cannot tell you that your child will return next month.
I cannot tell you that the prodigal story is a personalized prophecy guaranteeing the conversion of every wandering son or daughter.
I cannot give you a date.
I cannot give you a formula.
I cannot manipulate God with your parenting record.
But I can tell you what you can do today.
Remain faithful.
Keep praying.
Keep loving.
Keep repenting where repentance is needed.
Keep telling the truth.
Keep the door open where wisdom permits.
Keep refusing to turn Jesus into a weapon.
Keep trusting the character of God even when you cannot control the outcome.
And never confuse your inability to save your child with God's inability to reach your child.
Those are very different things.
There may be a mother reading this who has been crying quietly because her adult son laughs at Christianity now.
There may be a father reading this whose daughter wants nothing to do with church.
There may be grandparents watching a generation drift farther from everything they taught.
There may even be someone reading this who is the child who walked away.
If that's you, I want to speak to you for a moment.
Maybe Christianity became associated with wounds you never deserved.
Maybe Christians failed you badly.
Maybe your parents failed you.
Maybe a church failed you.
Those wounds matter.
But human hypocrisy cannot determine whether Jesus Christ is who He claimed to be.
Do not let somebody else's counterfeit keep you from investigating the real Christ.
Look at Jesus again.
Not the internet caricature.
Not merely the version presented by the worst Christian you have met.
Jesus.
The crucified Christ.
The risen Christ.
The Christ who confronted religious hypocrisy fiercely while receiving broken sinners.
The Christ who calls people not merely into religious affiliation but into repentance, faith, forgiveness, reconciliation, and new life.
And if you are the parent...
perhaps you need to release something tonight.
Not your child.
Your illusion of control.
You were never their Savior.
Jesus is.
Your job is not to become the Holy Spirit.
Your calling is to love Christ, obey Christ, teach His truth faithfully, repent when you fail, pray relentlessly, and bear witness to the Gospel.

Ephesians tells fathers not to provoke their children to anger but to bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord; Colossians similarly warns parents against embittering their children so they do not become discouraged.
Notice the balance.
Instruction without needless provocation.
Conviction without spiritual bullying.
Authority without crushing the soul.
Truth wrapped in a life that increasingly looks like Jesus.
And maybe that exposes something uncomfortable in us.
We desperately want our children to choose Christ.
But do they see that we choose Christ when choosing Him costs us something?
Do they see Jesus when we are insulted?
Do they see Him when money gets tight?
Do they see Him when someone wounds our pride?
Do they see us forgive?
Do they hear us confess?
Do they watch us put down the phone and open Scripture?
Do they see generosity that costs something?
Do they see us worship when life is painful?
Do they see Christianity as something we actually believe...
or merely something we attend?
Because Deuteronomy's vision was never faith performed once a week.
God's words were to permeate the home, the road, bedtime, morning—the ordinary fabric of life.
Maybe that is where revival in our children begins.
Not with louder Christian branding.
With deeper Christianity.
And if your child is already far away, do not waste your grief.
Let it drive you toward Jesus.
Let it expose your idols.
Even good things can become idols when we demand from them what only God can give.
Sometimes Christian parents quietly build their identity around raising “good Christian children.”
Then one child wanders and the parent's identity collapses.
But your ultimate identity cannot rest in your child's spiritual performance.
It must rest in Christ.
Otherwise you may begin loving your child as a project whose success proves your worth.
They will feel it.
Love them as a person made in God's image.
Tell them the truth because you love them.
Pray because you love them.
Listen because you love them.
Set necessary boundaries because you love them.
Refuse manipulation because you love them.
And entrust what you cannot control to God because you love Him.
Maybe someday the phone will ring.
Maybe someday the bedroom door will open.
Maybe someday your child will whisper something you have prayed years to hear.
“I need to talk.”
And maybe it will happen differently than you imagined.
But until then, don't build your faith on an ending God has not revealed.
Build it on Christ.
The cross already tells you that God takes sin seriously.
The cross already tells you that God's mercy is costly.
The resurrection already tells you that hopeless-looking situations are not beyond His power.
And the Gospel tells us something scandalous.
God saves sinners.
Not polished people.
Not children with perfect Christian résumés.
Sinners.
That includes rebellious children.
And exhausted parents.
That includes church kids who ran away.
And church parents who made terrible mistakes.
That includes the skeptic.
The hypocrite.
The ashamed.
The angry.
The religious.
The irreligious.
The prodigal.
And you.
This is why our message will always be From Scandal to Grace.
Because Jesus does not merely improve respectable people.
He redeems sinners.
He takes what sin shattered and begins making something new.
He brings confession where there was hiding.
Mercy where there was condemnation.
Truth where there were lies.
Life where there was death.
And no, this does not mean every earthly story receives the ending we demand.
It means Jesus Christ remains worthy of trust even while the final chapter is still being written.
So if your child has rejected God, tonight you can pray something simpler than all the frantic words you have been trying to find:

“Jesus, I cannot save my child. You are the Savior. Show me where I need to repent. Teach me how to love without compromising truth. Give me wisdom to speak and wisdom to remain silent. Protect my child from deception. Put faithful witnesses in their path. Open their eyes to Christ. And while I wait, keep my own heart from wandering away from You. Amen.”
And if you couldn't read that prayer without crying, you are not the only parent carrying this burden.
Someone reading this at 2:00 in the morning may desperately need to know that God is still at work.
There may be a night when fear returns and you need these truths again.
The Gospel cannot be bought. Salvation is God's gift in Christ.
Because sometimes the person who appears farthest from God is still reading.
Still thinking.
Still remembering.
Still hearing echoes of prayers prayed over them years ago.
And perhaps the parent who thinks the story is over is simply standing in a chapter where the ending cannot yet be seen.
You may not be able to write your child's next chapter—but you can keep pointing them to the Savior who still writes redemption into stories everyone else thought were finished.
